Q5: Reporting the software used to conduct the meta-analysis is important for several reasons. First, it allows other researchers to replicate the analysis and to verify the results. Second, it provides information about the capabilities and limitations of the software used, which can be helpful for other researchers when choosing software for their own meta-analyses. Third, it helps to ensure that the meta-analysis was conducted in a transparent and reproducible manner.
Q7: Reporting the packages used to conduct the meta-analysis is important for the same reasons as reporting the software used. Additionally, it can be helpful for other researchers to know which packages were used to conduct specific tasks in the meta-analysis, such as data extraction, data analysis, and visualization.
Q9: Reporting the version numbers of the software used to conduct the meta-analysis is important because different versions of software may have different features and functionality. By reporting the version numbers of the software used, other researchers can be sure that they are using the same software with the same features and functionality to replicate the meta-analysis.
Q11: Reporting the code used to conduct the meta-analysis is important for several reasons. First, it allows other researchers to replicate the analysis and to verify the results. Second, it provides information about the specific steps that were taken to conduct the meta-analysis, which can be helpful for other researchers when developing their own meta-analysis code. Third, it helps to ensure that the meta-analysis was conducted in a transparent and reproducible manner.
Q13: Reporting the primary model (or first model) used to conduct the meta-analysis is important because it allows other researchers to understand the specific assumptions that were made about the data and the statistical methods that were used. This information is essential for replicating the meta-analysis and for interpreting the results.
Q15: Reporting a justification for the primary model (or first model) used to conduct the meta-analysis is important because it helps other researchers to understand why the chosen model was the most appropriate one for the data and the research question. This information can be helpful for other researchers when choosing a model for their own meta-analyses.
Q17: Reporting a weighting scheme for effect size estimates in a meta-analysis is important because it allows other researchers to understand how the different studies in the meta-analysis were weighted relative to each other. This information is essential for interpreting the results of the meta-analysis.
Q19: Reporting whether there is non-independence of effect size estimates in a meta-analysis is important because non-independence can affect the validity of the results. By reporting whether there is non-independence, other researchers can be aware of this potential problem and can take steps to address it in their own meta-analyses.
Q21: Reporting a measure of heterogeneity between effect size estimates in a meta-analysis is important because it allows other researchers to understand how much the effect sizes vary across the studies in the meta-analysis. This information is essential for interpreting the results of the meta-analysis.
Q23: Reporting the moderator variables included in a meta-regression in a meta-analysis is important because it allows other researchers to understand how the effect sizes vary depending on the characteristics of the studies. This information can be helpful for identifying the factors that influence the effect size and for developing theories about the underlying mechanisms.
Q25: Reporting a sensitivity analysis in a meta-analysis is important because it allows other researchers to assess the robustness of the results to different assumptions and decisions. By reporting a sensitivity analysis, other researchers can be confident that the results of the meta-analysis are not simply due to the specific choices that were made in the analysis.
Q27: Reporting the total number of studies included in the meta-analysis is important because it allows readers to assess the comprehensiveness of the review and the size of the evidence base. This information is also essential for assessing the generalizability of the findings.

This isn't that directly quantifiable, but I believe a statement supporting what context(s) the meta-analysis really pertains to would be good. For example, a meta-analysis might be labelled as "global" (this is very common in my field) which actually means, the allowable *sources of literature* was global in scope. The actual *data* collected is very often not global -- e.g. studies might be concentrated in N. America, Europe, maybe Oceania, maybe some in Asia, but not at all in Africa. My opinion is that "global" is misleading here. What would be better would be to describe what conditions the meta-analysis really cover. For example, if studying responses across major soil orders of the world, report that "of the 32 world reference soil groups, the dataset compiled here represents 18 soil groups (Table X)". 
Relatedly, an assessment of *exchangeability* in observations is critical in my opinion. This is in context of multilevel models -- A. Gelman talks a bit about this, as does Richard McElreath. An example of the discussion of this issue in my general field is this paper by Eagle et al. (doi: 10.2134/agronj2017.04.0215). In other words, the observations being compared shouldn't be apples v. oranges.

Dogma leads to formulaic meta-analyses which stifle scientific creativity and critical thinking and which often fail to really progress the science.
Best of luck with this endeavour. If this can be a bit more applicable to the environmental sciences than other tools like PRISMA, then I can see this getting adopted fairly easily, which will be a great benefit to the field of evidence synthesis.
